spec.title: Holdout: routed accumulation and reported street flooding
spec.question: Do cells where people reported street flooding rank higher in routed flow accumulation than other cells of the same study area — and higher than simple low-elevation ranking?
spec.hypothesis: Pooled AUC of routed accumulation exceeds 0.5 and exceeds the low-elevation baseline, with the 95% cluster-bootstrap interval of the difference excluding zero.

conditions.routing: app model (v2 fill-and-spill); v1 D8 reported as secondary
conditions.forcing: Central Park gauge event rainfall × NLCD-derived runoff coefficient per area

spec.split: Holdout event fixed in experiments/PREREGISTRATION.md; evaluated once, after development-stage revisions were frozen (Addenda 1–2).
metrics: AUC (mean within-area mid-rank percentile of complaint cells)
paired difference with 95% cluster-bootstrap interval (areas resampled)
limitations: 311 complaints are reports, not measurements; absence of a report is not a dry observation.
Reporting depends on population, traffic and awareness, which also correlate with terrain.
Complaint coordinates are geocoded addresses, typically tens of metres from the flooded spot; cells are about 14 m.
One rain gauge stands for the whole city; event rainfall varied strongly across boroughs.
No sewer network is modelled, while NYC street flooding is largely sewer-capacity driven.
Land cover is uniform within each area, so spatial patterns come from terrain; the classifier is not tested here.

inputs.source: NYC 311 Service Requests from 2010 to Present
NYC Borough Boundaries (shoreline-clipped), NYC Department of City Planning
USGS National Land Cover Database 2021: land cover and percent developed imperviousness (CONUS)
NOAA NCEI Global Historical Climatology Network daily, Central Park (USW00094728)
Mapzen Terrarium tiles (AWS Terrain Tiles) and USGS 3DEP Bare Earth dynamic ImageServer
